newsitem.title: UK: Strong Euro stocks throw off Wall St shackles.
newsitem.headline: Strong Euro stocks throw off Wall St shackles.

text.p: Continental European stock markets threw off the shackles of Wall Street to flirt with record levels on Thursday, ignoring warnings from U.S. Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan.
London stocks were more cautious, although the FTSE index still closed modestly higher. The dollar survived a brief flutter when the Dutch central central bank announced an interest rate rise.

German and French stocks led the charge despite Greenspan's Wednesday warning against excessive optimism over the U.S. economy, and his hints that the Fed might raise interest rates to nip any inflation in the bud.
In Germany the DAX index closed up 1.2 percent or 38.85 points at a record 3,276.72, a fraction of a point higher than the previous high set on February 18.
In Paris, the picture was similar. The CAC-40 climbed to within a point of its record set earlier this month before slipping to finish up 1.05 percent or 27.23 points at 2,629.40.
French brokers welcomed signs that the Paris market was following domestic factors rather than Wall Street. "It's the de-coupling," one broker exclaimed.
The domestic factor on Thursday was encouraging data on Thursday showing GDP rose 0.2 percent in the fourth quarter of 1996, giving full-year growth of 1.3 percent.
"After Greenspan's statements and the drop on Wall Street, we were bracing for a decline today. But the GDP is a positive surprise," a Paris broker said.
London dealers were more sober, saying that Europe could not ignore any rise in U.S. rates and the FTSE index closed up a more modest 9.9 points at 4,339.2.
But still it largely ignored Wall Street, where the Dow Jones Industrial average was down 9.23 points at 6,973.95 at mid- morning.
"We haven't taken too much notice of Mr Greenspan ourselves, but it doesn't mean we will ignore any change in the interest rate environment there," said a senior London trader.
Most dealers believe the Fed will have to raise rates sooner or later but London traders were remaining calm.
"I think Wall Street will only correct when he puts rates up because there are real signs that the economy is growing too fast," said the head of British equities at one major fund management group.
British investors also had a domestic political factor in a parliamentary by-election on Thursday, in which the ruling Conservatives are expected to lose to the opposition Labour Party.
Traders wanted a clear-cut Labour victory to reduce the chance of no party winning decisively in the general election which has to be held by May.
The dollar closed lower in Europe but shrugged off the Dutch interest rate rise which raised concern whether the European trend of easing rates might be ending.
The Dutch central bank raised its key special advances rate to 2.70 percent from 2.50.
The dollar dipped initially to session lows but analysts said the rise was linked to the strong Dutch economy compared with Germany and its higher inflation.
"You would have to be seriously paranoid to think the Dutch rate hike is a harbinger for European rates to go up," said Tony Norfield, treasury economist at ABN Amro.
At the European close, the dollar stood at 1.6890 marks and 120.76 yen, little changed from 1.6895 in late trading on Wednesday but down from 122.15 yen.
Worries about profit-taking and fiscal year-end repatriation of funds in Japan lifted the yen.

Stronger than expected Japanese industrial production data overnight and the belief that Japanese and U.S. authorities would intevene if the dollar moved over 125 yen also boosted the Japanese currency.
Comments by Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer about Europen monetary union and the dollar had little effect.
Tietmeyer painted a gloomy picture of the prospects for EMU if two key requirements, a stable single currency and lasting budget restraint, were not met.
Prices of rare precious metals platinum and palladium leapt on fears there could be strike at Russia's huge Norilsk production facility in Arctic Siberia.
Later they eased as speculators took profits, but at the London morning fixing platinum was up $10.00 at $393.50 per ounce, its highest fix since September.
CURRENCIES AT EUROPEAN CLOSE
The dollar was at 1.6890 marks and 120.76 yen, compared with 1.6895 and 122.15 in late European trade on Wednesday.
STOCK MARKETS AT CLOSE
LONDON - The FTSE-100 index closed up 9.9 points at 4,339.2.
PARIS - The CAC-40 closed 27.23 points higher at 2,629.40.
FRANKFURT - The 30-share DAX index closed floor trade up 38.85 points at a record 3,276.72. In later screen-based trade the IBIS DAX index was up 27.56 at 3,272.58.
PRECIOUS METALS
Gold closed at $360.65 compared with $353.85 at the London close on Wednesday. Silver was three cents higher at $5.26.
